title: Why teachers stay
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes reframes teacher retention by asking not why teachers leave but what makes them want to stay, arguing structural surveys about vacancy rates and exit interviews miss the daily emotional experience of belonging that keeps career teachers in schools. Drawing on interviews with hundreds of 20+ year career teachers for her forthcoming book with Sam Gibbs, 'Love the One You're With', she reports that belonging, not money or holidays, was the strongest factor in retention, and applies Steele and Murphy's concept of 'situated belonging' to argue people constantly scan school environments for cues about whether their identity will be trusted or overlooked. She warns that professional development often carries an unintended message of suspicion rather than investment, and closes by urging schools to audit their PD, coaching and progression structures through a belonging lens rather than assuming a busy CPD calendar equals a supportive culture.
points: Hughes's headline finding from interviews with hundreds of career teachers - that belonging, not money or holidays, was the biggest factor in long-term retention - reframes the retention debate away from pay and toward culture.

She applies Steele and Murphy's 'situated belonging' concept to argue staff constantly scan institutional cues (representation, norms, language) for signals about whether they will be trusted, a lens usually reserved for students.
Her anecdote about a head of department reacting to an offer of coaching with 'What have I done wrong?' vividly illustrates how PD can unintentionally signal suspicion rather than investment.
She rejects simplistic 'novice vs expert' categories for teacher development, arguing growth needs are role-, stage- and context-sensitive rather than following one neat sequence.
quotes: A better question might be this: what makes teachers want to stay? Retention is emotional as well as structural, belonging is not a soft extra and the culture adults experience shapes the culture pupils inherit.

We interviewed hundreds of career teachers (20+ years) about what had helped them stay in the profession. Spoiler alert, it wasn't money or the holidays. Belonging and feeling part of a bigger mission was by far the biggest factor.
Classic case in point is that in my trust I offered a head of department some coaching and her initial reaction was What have I done wrong? This spoke volumes about the culture in the school to me.
A process that was meant to signal support starts to signal suspicion. A structure meant to help people grow starts telling them that they are not trusted to think.

Teachers do not stay because there is a CPD booklet. They stay because the culture beneath that booklet keeps telling them, in credible ways, that they are accepted, that they matter, that they can contribute, that they can grow, and that their judgement is trusted.
